questions.stem: A colorimeter determines rate by measuring

options.text: The amount of light passing through the solution at intervals
options.explanation: Falling or rising light intensity tracks concentration change.

options.text: The mass of the reaction vessel
options.explanation: Mass belongs to the mass-loss method.
Volume belongs to the gas-collection method.
Temperature is controlled, not measured as the rate signal.

questions.stem: The plotted detector readings represent concentration against time because

options.text: Colour is always independent of concentration
options.explanation: The method relies on the opposite.

options.text: Light intensity reaching the detector is related to the concentration of the coloured species
options.explanation: Absorbance and concentration move together, making intensity a proxy.
Different quantities entirely.
No such heating is involved.

questions.stem: Colorimetry is unsuitable for a reaction that forms a coloured precipitate because

options.explanation: No such dissolving occurs.

options.text: The detector cannot see any colour at all
options.explanation: Colour is visible; the trouble is scattering.

options.text: Suspended particles scatter or block the light, corrupting the intensity reading
options.explanation: The optical path degrades, so intensity no longer tracks concentration cleanly.
Speed is not the problem.

questions.stem: For a coloured reactant monitored by colorimetry, the sketch graph of colour intensity against time

options.explanation: A reactant's colour cannot rise while it is consumed.
A horizontal line would mean no reaction.
Clean kinetics data smooth such noise.

options.text: Falls as the reactant is used up
options.explanation: The coloured species is consumed, so intensity drops.

questions.stem: Detector readings are taken every few seconds so that

options.text: Enough points exist to draw a smooth concentration-time curve and read gradients
options.explanation: Frequent sampling gives the curve its shape.
Lamp life is irrelevant to sampling.
Sampling does not alter kinetics.
One reading cannot yield a rate.

questions.stem: State what a colorimeter measures and how often readings are taken.
questions.modelAnswer: It measures the light intensity passing through the solution, logged every few seconds.

questions.stem: State the limitation that stops colorimetry following precipitate formation.
questions.modelAnswer: Coloured precipitates scatter or block the light, so the detector reading no longer represents concentration.

questions.stem: Explain why light intensity can stand in for concentration in colorimetry.
questions.modelAnswer: The colour of a solution deepens with the concentration of the coloured species, so the light absorbed, and therefore the intensity reaching the detector, changes in step with concentration.

questions.stem: A reaction turns a clear solution progressively yellow. Describe how you would obtain a rate graph from this mixture.
questions.modelAnswer: Run the mixture in a colorimeter, log the rising absorbance of the yellow species every few seconds, convert absorbance to concentration with a calibration curve, and plot concentration against time.

questions.stem: Mass loss can follow a reaction rate only when

options.explanation: Enthalpy plays no role here.

options.text: A gas is produced that is dense enough to register on the balance
options.explanation: The method's resolution depends on a substantial mass change.
Colour is the colorimetry signal.
Precipitates stay in the vessel and do not change the mass.

questions.stem: In the calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid experiment, the mass decreases because

options.explanation: The solid converts to products, some of which escape as gas.
A calibrated balance does not drift by design.

options.text: Carbon dioxide escapes from the vessel as the reaction proceeds
options.explanation: The gaseous product leaves, taking its mass with it.
Evaporation is not the intended cause.

questions.stem: Hydrogen is a poor gas for the mass-loss method because

options.explanation: No such reaction occurs.
Hydrogen is colourless, which is irrelevant here.

options.text: It dissolves completely in the acid
options.explanation: Dissolution is not the stated limitation.

options.text: Its molar mass of 2 makes the mass change too small for a 2 or 3 dp balance
options.explanation: The lost mass per mole is tiny, so readings barely move.

questions.stem: The graph of mass loss against time is equivalent to a graph of

options.explanation: Mass lost measures how much material has reacted away.

options.text: Amount of product present in the vessel
options.explanation: The gaseous product has left, so it is not present to measure.
Temperature is not plotted here.

options.text: Concentration of the gas inside the vessel
options.explanation: The gas escapes, so its internal concentration is not what the balance reads.

questions.stem: Mass readings are taken every few seconds during the experiment in order to

options.explanation: The whole method is graphical.

options.text: Give enough points to plot the mass-time curve and read the rate from its gradient
options.explanation: Rate comes from the slope of the plotted curve.
Calibration is separate from sampling.
Weighing does not warm anything.

questions.stem: State which gas is suitable for the mass-loss method and which is not.
questions.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide (Mr = 44) is dense enough for the method; hydrogen (Mr = 2) is not.

questions.stem: State what is plotted in the mass-loss method.
questions.modelAnswer: The change in mass of the vessel and contents, measured every few seconds, plotted against time.

questions.stem: Explain why the mass-loss graph doubles as a reactant-amount graph.
questions.modelAnswer: Each gram of mass lost is exactly the gas that has formed from the reactants and left the vessel, so the cumulative loss measures how much reactant material has been consumed by that moment.

questions.stem: A student proposes the mass-loss method for magnesium reacting with dilute acid to give hydrogen. Evaluate the proposal.
questions.modelAnswer: Hydrogen's molar mass of 2 makes the mass change too small for a balance reading to 2 or 3 decimal places, so the proposal is weak; a gas syringe measuring the hydrogen volume is the better choice.

questions.stem: The gas-volume method measures rate by

options.explanation: That is the colorimetry method.
That is the quenching route of the next lesson.

options.text: Trapping the product gas and recording its volume at intervals
options.explanation: Growing volume marks product formation over time.
That is the mass-loss method.

questions.stem: The alternative set-up bubbles gas through water into an inverted measuring cylinder, but only when

options.explanation: Colour is irrelevant to collection.

options.text: The gas is denser than air
options.explanation: Density against air does not govern this set-up.
Enthalpy plays no role in the choice.

options.text: The gas is not water soluble
options.explanation: Dissolution would steal gas from the measured volume.

questions.stem: In the magnesium and hydrochloric acid example, the gas collected is

options.explanation: Magnesium plus acid liberates hydrogen.
Carbonates give carbon dioxide; magnesium is not a carbonate.
No oxygen is produced by this reaction.
Chloride stays as chloride ions in solution.

questions.stem: The graph of gas volume evolved against time represents

options.explanation: Temperature is not the measured variable.
Volume collected measures product formed.
Reactant amount is inferred by subtraction, not read directly.
The axes are volume and time.

questions.stem: Readings of gas volume are taken every few seconds so that

options.explanation: Reading a volume never changes the chemistry.
Intermediate points carry the rate information.

options.text: A smooth volume-time curve can be plotted and its gradient read as the rate
options.explanation: Gradients need a well-populated curve.

options.text: The gas stays in the syringe
options.explanation: Sampling does not trap the gas.

questions.stem: State the two collection arrangements for measuring gas volume.
questions.modelAnswer: A gas syringe collecting the gas directly, or an inverted measuring cylinder over water.

questions.stem: State the condition for using the inverted measuring cylinder over water.
questions.modelAnswer: The gas must not be water soluble, or it would dissolve instead of being collected.

questions.stem: Explain why gas volume serves as a stand-in for amount of product.
questions.modelAnswer: At a fixed temperature and pressure the volume of a gas is proportional to the number of moles present, so every increment of collected volume corresponds to a fixed amount of product formed.

questions.stem: A reaction gives off ammonia, which dissolves readily in water. Which gas-volume arrangement should be avoided, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: The inverted measuring cylinder over water should be avoided, because dissolving ammonia would remove gas from the collected volume and understate the rate; a gas syringe is the appropriate choice.

questions.stem: Quenching a sample means

options.text: Cooling the sample to room temperature only
options.explanation: Cooling alone does not stop the chemistry.
Dilution is not the definition.
Filtration is not the definition.

options.text: Deliberately stopping the reaction in that sample so analysis does not change the reading
options.explanation: A quenched sample is frozen at its quench-moment composition.

questions.stem: After quenching, the sample's concentration is obtained by

options.explanation: Titration reads the quenched concentration.
Precipitates defeat colorimetry.
Mass is not concentration.
Gas volume is a different method.

questions.stem: The disappearing-cross experiment works because

options.explanation: The cross sits outside the flask; the solution clouds.

options.text: The forming sulfur precipitate gradually obscures a cross viewed through the mixture, giving a repeatable endpoint
options.explanation: The visual endpoint is the timing signal.
No magnetism is involved.
Acidity is not the signal.

questions.stem: Stopping the clock at a visible point such as complete dissolution of magnesium is useful because

options.text: It works for reactions with no visible change
options.explanation: Visibility is the whole requirement.

options.text: It removes the need for a stopwatch
options.explanation: A stopwatch is exactly what is used.

options.text: It times a fixed extent of reaction without any sampling or titration
options.explanation: A visible endpoint replaces instrumental monitoring.
The clock measures time, not concentration.

questions.stem: Taking a sample for titration without quenching risks

options.explanation: Evaporation is not the stated risk.

options.text: The titrant reacting with the flask
options.explanation: The titrant meets the sample, not the flask.
Samples of reacting mixtures are not stable.

options.text: The reaction continuing in the sample after removal, corrupting the concentration reading
options.explanation: Unquenched samples keep reacting during handling.

questions.stem: State what quenching does to a removed sample.
questions.modelAnswer: Quenching deliberately stops the reaction in the sample so that its composition is frozen for analysis.

questions.stem: Name the observation that signals the endpoint in the thiosulfate-acid clock experiment.
questions.modelAnswer: The yellow sulfur precipitate formed obscures a cross viewed through the solution.

questions.stem: Explain why titration of an unquenched sample gives an unreliable concentration.
questions.modelAnswer: The sample keeps reacting between removal and analysis, so the concentration measured by titration belongs to the analysis moment rather than the removal moment, corrupting the time-concentration pair.

questions.stem: A reaction mixture is colourless throughout and gives off no gas. Outline a workable rate measurement plan.
questions.modelAnswer: Remove samples at timed intervals, quench each one, and titrate to read concentration; plotting the quenched concentrations against their removal times builds the concentration-time curve.
